content:
According to a 404 Media report, Magnet Forensics says it has found a way to bypass a security feature on the iPhone. The feature automatically restarts the device when it has not been unlocked for 72 consecutive hours. Details are as follows.

First, some background.

Just under two years ago, the iOS 18.1 update introduced a feature called "Inactivity Reboot." If an iPhone is not unlocked for 72 consecutive hours, the system forces a restart.

This feature basically makes it harder for law enforcement agencies and forensic tools to access the data on a locked iPhone, because after a restart the device returns to a "Before First Unlock" (BFU) state, rather than staying in the less restricted "After First Unlock" (AFU) state.

When an iPhone is in the BFU state, some sensitive data is still protected by encryption keys. The user has to enter the passcode for the first time before these keys are released, and only then does the device enter the AFU state.

From that moment, more data on the device becomes accessible, and it stays in that state until the iPhone restarts again, at which point it returns to BFU.

The fact that an iPhone restarts automatically means that even if law enforcement has not yet seized the device, the phone could have already returned to the BFU state before investigators get their hands on it — because obtaining a search warrant or sending the device to a forensic lab both take time.

When iOS 18.1 was released, 404 Media already pointed out that this feature also makes it harder for thieves or other bad actors to keep a stolen iPhone in the AFU state for an extended period, in order to study or exploit vulnerabilities to break into the device.

Report: GrayKey has bypassed the Inactivity Reboot feature.

Reporting today, 404 Media says that, according to a tutorial and demonstration video "produced for law enforcement and apparently dated early 2025," Magnet Forensics, the developer of the GrayKey phone-unlocking tool, appears to have developed a way to bypass the iPhone's Inactivity Reboot feature.

The report says Magnet has developed a new device called GrayKey Preserve, and has also added an "Evidence Preservation Mode" to its existing GrayKey hardware.

Both are said to be designed to preserve the forensic state of an iPhone without having to immediately read the data stored on the device, allowing law enforcement to maintain that state unchanged while waiting for search authorisation.

The report notes that, although the video does not go into the technical details of the bypass mechanism, it does explain that GrayKey can keep the iPhone in its AFU state even after a restart.

Report details:

404 Media reached out separately to both Apple and Magnet Forensics, and neither responded to a request for comment. They also consulted iPhone security researcher Jiska Classen, who said Magnet may have found a way to tamper with the iPhone's clock, or to simply disable the mechanism responsible for expiring certain data.

Although the video appears to date from early 2025, it is not clear how long this technology has been made available to law enforcement, whether it has been used in actual investigations, or whether it still works against the latest version of iOS.
